title: Ph.D. Project: Holistic Partitioning and Optimization of CPU-FPGA Applications Through Source-to-Source Compilation
problem: Hardware/software partitioning and High-level Synthesis (HLS) optimization are typically applied independently without leveraging their potential interplay. This leads to suboptimal offloading decisions that don't account for how partitioning choices affect optimization opportunities and vice versa.
motivation: Efficiently accelerating performance-critical software regions onto FPGAs requires joint optimization of partitioning and synthesis decisions to maximize hardware efficiency and minimize communication overhead.
method: The approach automatically converts C/C++ code into an Extended Task Graph (ETG), breaking the program into individual tasks. It then groups these tasks into clusters for an FPGA (a reconfigurable chip optimized for specific workloads), while simultaneously balancing three objectives: applying the hardware's available optimizations within each cluster, reducing data traffic between the CPU and FPGA, and keeping tasks that access the same data together.
key_novelty: Instead of separately deciding how to split work between CPU and FPGA and then optimizing each piece, this approach handles both simultaneously through source-to-source compilation, allowing partitioning choices to directly influence available optimizations.
contributions: Holistic framework integrating hw/sw partitioning with HLS optimization
Source-to-source compilation automation for CPU-FPGA co-design
Extended Task Graph representation for analyzing C/C++ applications
Multi-objective clustering algorithm balancing optimization potential, communication cost, and data locality
limitations: Not discussed; paper is presented as work-in-progress with no experimental validation or results provided.
primary_theme: Unified partitioning and optimization for CPU-FPGA systems
